pedagogy.summary: This topic turns coordinate reading into PRODUCING: given coordinates, plot the point on the grid; and given a shape's structure, work out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. It is a two-way translation between the symbolic pair (x, y) and the spatial mark on the grid — reading a pair to place a point, and reading a placed configuration to generate a new coordinate. Completing a polygon (find the 4th vertex of a square, the 3rd of a triangle) is where coordinates meet shape properties: the missing vertex of a rectangle/square shares one known vertex's x-value and another's y-value. The dominant error, as in reading, is reversal (plotting up-then-across); the second is completing a shape 'by eye' from appearance rather than reasoning from the coordinates.
bestPractices: Plot with the same along-then-up discipline as reading: find the x-line first, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection — count from the origin against numbered lines.

For a missing vertex, reason from coordinates and shape properties, not appearance: the 4th vertex of a rectangle takes its x from one neighbour and its y from the other; verify sides are the right lengths.
Have children state the missing coordinate BEFORE plotting it, so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.
Draw the sides in order and check the result is the intended polygon (right angles for a rectangle, equal sides for a square), catching mis-plotted vertices.
Contrast a correctly completed square with a plausible-looking wrong one to show that 'looks right' is not the test — the coordinates are.
Use the reversal distractor deliberately: plot (5,4) and (4,5) to show they are different, reinforcing order in the act of plotting.
keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with origin, points plotted as line-intersections
Along-then-up plotting path from the origin to each point
Partly-drawn polygon with given vertices and one missing, to be completed
The missing vertex sharing one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y (rectangle/square)
Completed shape with all vertex coordinates labelled
commonMisconceptions: Reversal when plotting — going up before across, so the point lands in the mirror position (e.g. plots (5,4) at 4-across-5-up).
Completing a polygon by eye/appearance rather than reasoning from coordinates and shape properties, giving a wrong missing vertex.
Counting squares instead of numbered lines when plotting, producing off-by-one positions.
Joining vertices in the wrong order, producing a crossed or incorrect polygon even when the points are right.

learn.summary: This topic moves children from reading coordinates to PRODUCING them: given a pair (x, y), plot the point; given a partly-drawn polygon, reason out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. The key reasoning is that the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines shares one neighbour's x-value and another neighbour's y-value, so completion is derived from coordinates and shape properties rather than guessed by eye. The two dominant errors are reversal (plotting up-then-across) and completing 'by eye' from appearance instead of reasoning from the coordinates.

activities.title: Plot-and-complete on a numbered grid
feedback: If a plotted point lands reversed, return to along-then-up plotting from the origin, tie the first number to the across axis, and plot (5,1) and (1,5) together to show they differ.
If the fourth vertex is placed by eye (near but not at the target), ask the child to say which neighbour's x and which neighbour's y it must share, then check side lengths and right angles.
If points land one line off, anchor at the origin (0,0) and count the numbered line labels aloud while placing the point, rather than counting cells crossed.

When the drawn sides form a leaning or lopsided quadrilateral, point out that the coordinates, side lengths and right angles, not the appearance, are the test — four equal sides and four right angles for a square, equal opposite sides and four right angles for a rectangle.
activities.rationale: Plotting and completing a polygon is a produce-and-check action: entering a point and drawing the sides gives spatial feedback that exposes reversal (the point visibly lands wrong) and by-eye completion (the figure fails to close into the named shape, or the side lengths are unequal). Stating the coordinate before plotting makes the reasoning explicit and checkable.
sourceClaims: Students graph points in the first quadrant to represent problems and interpret coordinate values, locating each point by an ordered pair measured from the origin along the two axes (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
Year 4 pupils should plot specified points and draw sides to complete a given polygon.

A common documented misconception is putting the y-coordinate before the x, giving an incorrectly placed point; the Year 4 objective works on a grid where the lines are numbered (reading numbered lines rather than counting squares). Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.
learnerActions: Plot a given point by finding the x-line first, travelling up to the y-line, and marking the intersection, counting from the origin against the numbered lines.
Plot (5,4) and then (4,5) and compare: show they land in different places to make the along-then-up order explicit.

Given three vertices of a genuine square, e.g. (1,1), (1,4) and (4,4) (whose fourth vertex is (4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides), STATE the fourth coordinate aloud before plotting it, then plot it and draw the sides; check all four side lengths are equal and all four corners are right angles so the figure is genuinely a square.
Check the completed figure is the intended polygon: right angles and matching opposite sides for a rectangle, right angles and four equal sides for a square.

Repeat with three vertices of a rectangle, e.g. (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) whose fourth vertex is (5,1), giving a 4-by-3 rectangle, so the shared-x / shared-y reasoning transfers and children see that unequal sides (4 and 3) make a rectangle, not a square.
activities.intendedInsight: A point's location is fixed by reading x (across) then y (up) from the origin, and the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines can be reasoned out because it shares one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y; 'looks right' is replaced by 'is right' when the drawn sides form the named shape, with right angles at every corner and matching side lengths — four equal sides for a square, equal opposite sides for a rectangle.

activities.title: Which coordinate completes the shape? — diagnostic choices
feedback: If the reversed pair is chosen, revisit along-then-up order and compare the swapped pair with the correct one on a grid.
If the by-eye value is chosen, ask which neighbour supplies the x and which supplies the y for the missing corner, then check the side lengths.
If points are joined in the wrong order producing a crossed figure, draw the sides in vertex order and check the shape closes correctly.
activities.rationale: Choosing the correct missing vertex is cleanly scorable and useful for diagnosis, with the reversed pair and the by-eye value as targeted distractors. On its own this recognition format does not elicit the child independently plotting and drawing to see the sides close, so pair it with a grid where the child produces and checks.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is putting the y-coordinate before the x, giving an incorrectly placed point; the Year 4 objective works on a grid where the lines are numbered (reading numbered lines rather than counting squares). Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.
learnerActions: Choose which coordinate completes a given genuine square, e.g. three vertices (1,1),(1,4),(4,4) whose correct fourth vertex is (4,1), from options that include the reversed pair and a plausible but wrong by-eye value.
Explain WHY the chosen coordinate is correct in terms of shared x and shared y, not appearance.
Match a set of plotted points to their coordinate labels.
Plot a given set of points to form a rectangle and join them in order.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying the correct missing vertex, and rejecting the reversal and by-eye distractors, shows that the vertex is determined by the coordinates and shape structure, not by how the figure looks.

activities.title: Reveal how a completed shape's coordinates relate
feedback: If a prediction is wrong, show which neighbour supplies the x and which supplies the y and re-trace the plotting path.
Prompt the child to state the shared-value reasoning before revealing the answer so the pattern, not the picture, is used.
activities.rationale: A static or worked grid can display the structural relationship between vertices and let the child predict before revealing, which supports the shared-x/shared-y reasoning. It is a scaffold: a fixed figure cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so the producing that defines this topic still needs an interactive or paper grid where the child plots their own points and draws the sides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should plot specified points and draw sides to complete a given polygon.
learnerActions: On a completed rectangle with all vertices labelled, tap each corner to reveal how its coordinates relate to its neighbours (which x it shares, which y it shares).
Before a 'where must the fourth corner go?' answer is revealed, predict the coordinate and give a reason based on the shared values.
Trace the along-then-up path from the origin to each labelled vertex.
activities.intendedInsight: Even on a worked, labelled figure the child can see the structural pattern — each vertex shares an x with one neighbour and a y with another — which is the reasoning needed to complete a polygon.

constraints: Plot with along-then-up discipline: find the x-line, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection; count from the origin against the numbered lines, not by counting squares.

Completion must be reasoned from coordinates and shape properties (shared x and shared y of neighbours, for shapes whose sides run along the grid lines), not from appearance; verify side lengths and right angles — four equal sides with four right angles confirm a square, equal opposite sides with four right angles a rectangle.
Have children state the missing coordinate before plotting it so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the missing vertex, matching labels) are good for diagnosis but do not by themselves show the child independently plotting and drawing the sides to see the figure close; pair them with a produce-and-draw task.
A worked, labelled figure is a scaffold: it shows the relationship but cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so include a grid (interactive or paper) where the child plots and draws.
First-quadrant plotting and completing plane polygons is a 2D task; include the zero-coordinate/axis case, e.g. compare (3,0) and (0,3) as distinct points.

When a point set is named a square, confirm it actually has four equal sides; a set like (1,1),(1,4),(5,4),(5,1) has unequal sides (4 and 3) and is a rectangle, so use it as a rectangle example and reserve 'square' for equal-sided sets such as (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Optional interaction examples retained from the source (type a coordinate to drop a point with an along-then-up trail, snap-to-numbered-lines with origin highlighted, a complete-the-polygon mode that draws the sides and names the resulting shape, (5,4) vs (4,5) order check) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and are not mandatory.

The source's '3D adds no value' and 'dialogue cannot teach plotting' claims were not propagated as universal laws; 2D plotting is the natural medium for this content, but no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.

Corrected original error: the point set (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) with fourth vertex (5,1) forms a RECTANGLE 4 units wide and 3 units tall (sides 4 and 3), NOT a square. The derivation is sound — the fourth vertex shares x=5 with (5,4) and y=1 with (1,1) — but the original row's diagnostic prompt and correctAnswer mislabel the resulting figure a 'square' (its own evidence list correctly calls the identical set a rectangle). Guidance now treats this set as a rectangle example and supplies a genuine square example (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides.

probeDeeper: 'How did you know the fourth corner was (5,1) and not somewhere else?' — listen for 'it shares this x and that y', not 'it looked right'.
Counterexample: 'If I move this corner from (5,1) to (5,2), is it still a square? Why not?' — tests that the coordinates, not appearance, define the shape.
'Here are three corners of a rectangle instead of a square — where does the fourth go?' — checks the shared-x/shared-y reasoning transfers.
'Plot (3,0) and (0,3) — are they the same point?' — surfaces order and the zero-coordinate/axis case during producing.
assess.correctAnswer: READ: each point is located across (x) then up (y) from the origin — e.g. (5,4) is 5 across, 4 up. PRODUCE: the fourth vertex is (5,1) — it shares the x-value (5) of (5,4) and the y-value (1) of (1,1); plotted at 5-across-1-up, completing the square with vertical and horizontal sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal when plotting — plots the fourth vertex (or reads a given one) up-before-across, placing (5,1) at 1-across-5-up.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to along-then-up plotting from the origin, tying the first number to the x (across) axis; plot (5,1) and (1,5) together to show they differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The plotted point is the coordinate-swap of the correct one; the drawn figure is not a square; reading of the given vertices may also swap across and up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Completes the polygon by eye — places the fourth vertex where it 'looks right' rather than reasoning from the coordinates and the square's properties.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from structure: the missing vertex of a rectangle/square shares one neighbour's x and the other's y; check side lengths and right angles rather than trusting appearance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fourth point is near but not at (5,1); the child can't say it should share (5,4)'s x and (1,1)'s y; the drawn shape is a rough quadrilateral, not a square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares not numbered lines — plots off-by-one, or starts from 1 instead of the origin.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor at the origin (0,0) and plot on the numbered lines; count line labels aloud while placing the point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points land one line off; the child counts cells crossed rather than reading the line labels.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot plot given points reliably or complete the polygon: points land reversed or off-by-one, no missing vertex, or a shape that isn't the target.
responseLevels.full: Reads each given vertex as (across, up), derives the missing vertex from the shared x and y of its neighbours, plots it accurately on the numbered lines, and draws sides that form the correct polygon — reading and producing coordinates fluently in both directions.
responseLevels.partial: Plots the given vertices correctly (can read the marks) but cannot PRODUCE the missing vertex by reasoning — guesses by eye, or reverses when plotting the new point — so the completed figure is not a true square; reads but does not fully translate to producing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a grid with three vertices of a square marked and labelled: (1,1), (1,4) and (5,4). First (READ): 'Point to each marked vertex and tell me what its two numbers mean.' Then (PRODUCE): 'Plot the fourth vertex to complete the square, write its coordinates, and draw the sides.' Watch both the reading and the plotting.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task requires BOTH translating a symbol to a location (reading the given vertices) and generating a new symbol from a spatial/structural constraint (the missing vertex). A child who can read but not produce plots by eye and misses (5,1); a child who reverses lands the fourth vertex at (1,5); a child reasoning correctly derives it from the shared x and y. Drawing the sides then exposes whether the figure is actually a square, catching by-appearance completion.
